new_statements.quote: All these examples are given as they occur in an intonational phrase with penultimate vowel length. Nambya, as shown in (7), shows a predictable penultimate lengthening realised on different morphemes as causative and applicative suffixes are added: ku-se:k-a 'to laugh' (se´ka´), ku-sek-e:s-a 'to cause to laugh', ku-sek-e:l-a 'to laugh at', ku-sek-el-e:l-a 'to cause to laugh at'
new_statements.citation: Nyoni, Vincent & Geoffrey Kazembe Tambulukani. 2025. Analysis of tone patterns in Nambya language of Hwange District in Matabeleland North Province, Zimbabwe. Journal of Languages and Linguistics 4(1): 76-90. doi:10.51317/jll.v4i1.834
new_statements.locator: p. 86, section on verb tone (examples (6)-(7), Table 18)
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Nambya is a two-tone (H/L) Bantu language; word-level prominence is described only as predictable lengthening of the penultimate vowel of the (intonational-)phrase-final word, which stays on the penult as suffixes are added (ku-se:ka, ku-seke:sa, ku-sekele:la). No source opened uses 'stress' for a position; Downing & Gick 2001: 71 only note that the first syllable of #CuuCV... words is 'unstressed'. Provisional catalog reading if lengthening is taken as the stress exponent: fixed penultimate.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Companion paper (Nyoni & Tambulukani 2025 AQSSR: 731) repeats: 'The language exhibits predictable penultimate lengthening across various verbal extensions, including the intensive, applicative, reciprocal, causative, passive and stative (potential) forms.' Nyoni & Tambulukani 2024 IJSRA: 1029 say long vowels are otherwise restricted to certain tense forms (future, some negatives).
new_statements.domain_note: Phrase-level: lengthening is stated for words 'in an intonational phrase' (phrase-final position), i.e. the usual Bantu penultimate lengthening, not a claim about citation-form word stress; tone is the contrastive prosody. Data are the authors' own fieldwork with ten Hwange-district speakers.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe the Nambya of Hwange District, Zimbabwe (Downing & Gick's consultant also from Hwange) = namb1291 itself; no separately named dialect. Older literature (Doke 1931, Guthrie) treats Nambya/'Nambzya' as a Kalanga (kala1384) dialect; the Kalanga catalog entry (Mathangwane 1996) is a different language-level entry and was not used here.

sources.note: No word 'stress'; states that verb examples 'are given as they occur in an intonational phrase with penultimate vowel length' and that Nambya 'shows a predictable penultimate lengthening' as causative/applicative suffixes are added (p. 86). Tone (H/L) is the lexical/grammatical contrast.

sources.note: No text layer; scanned (tesseract 300 dpi,.). Only mention, methods aside p. 71: target /f/ tokens 'occur word-internally, in the context #Cu_uCV..., with the first syllable of the word unstressed' — implies word stress exists and is non-initial, no position stated. Nambya data = Downing field notes (Hwange speaker at UZ, 2000).
